data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Kiribati uses the Australian dollar, so it has no monetary policy at all - inflation is whatever Australia and world food-fuel prices deliver. The result is extreme volatility for a micro-economy: 13.7% in 2008, deflation of -3.9% in 2010, -3% in 2012, then 9.8% in 2009 and 9.3% in 2023 on global shocks. The IMF projects 6.5% for 2025, still elevated. Price stability is structurally impossible to manage domestically; the only buffers are fiscal - the Revenue Equalization Stabilization Fund and fishing-license windfalls that let the government smooth household costs through subsidies when import prices spike.
debt_management: Kiribati barely borrows: gross debt peaked at 21.2% of GDP in 2016 and has fallen to a projected 8% in 2025, the series low. The fiscal story is the opposite of most Pacific islands - tuna fishing-license revenues under the Vessel Day Scheme turned the budget structurally strong through the 2010s, and the RERF sovereign wealth fund (built from earlier phosphate wealth) provides a cushion worth several times GDP. Debt sustainability is not the question; the question is whether fishing revenues, which depend on tuna migration patterns shifting with ocean warming, hold up.

key_events.event: September: switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China, deepening Beijing's Pacific footprint.
President Maamau re-elected in June, consolidating the pro-China foreign policy turn.
Reopened the Phoenix Islands Protected Area to commercial fishing, trading conservation for revenue.
COVID-19 arrived after a long virus-free stretch, ending one of the world's strictest border closures.

outlook_next_decade: Kiribati's finances are the strongest in the Pacific on paper, but the economy is an existential bet on sea-level rise: much of the country sits under two meters above the ocean. Fishing revenues should stay strong near-term, funding adaptation and the RERF. The strategic risk is geopolitical - Kiribati's location and its China ties make it a pawn in great-power competition, which could either bring investment or instability. Macroeconomically, the decade looks stable; physically, it is the most threatened nation on earth.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
